tracks.name: App Router Basics
tracks.description: Pages, layouts, and navigation in the Next.js App Router.

lessons.title: 1. A page is a component
lessons.summary: Every folder in app/ becomes a route; page.js is what renders there.

activities.title: The route is the file
activities.instruction: `app/page.js` exports a React component and answers `/`. There is no route table to edit — the folder structure is the route table.

activities.title: Which file wins
activities.question: Which file renders at the root URL `/` in the App Router?
activities.explanation: `layout.js` wraps pages but is not a page itself. `pages/` belongs to the older Pages Router.

activities.title: Write the home page
activities.instruction: Export a default `HomePage` component from `app/page.js` that renders a `main` with an `h1` saying 'Welcome to the shop'.

teaching.text: In the App Router a folder is a URL segment. A folder with a `page.js` is a route; a folder with only a `layout.js` is just a wrapper for the routes inside it.
The default export is required. A named export called `Page` renders nothing, which is a common and silent mistake.

lessons.task: Export a default component from app/page.js rendering an h1.
hints: Export a function as default and return JSX.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does adding a folder to app/ not automatically create a working route?

lessons.title: 2. Nested routes
lessons.summary: Nesting folders nests URLs, one page file per segment.

activities.title: Folders map to paths
activities.instruction: `app/about/page.js` answers `/about`. `app/shop/shoes/page.js` answers `/shop/shoes`. No configuration, no router file.

activities.title: Folder without a page
activities.question: `app/dashboard/settings/layout.js` exists but there is no `page.js`. What does `/dashboard/settings` return?
choices: A 404 — a segment needs a page to be a route
activities.answer: A 404 — a segment needs a page to be a route
activities.explanation: Layouts wrap pages. With no page at that segment, the URL has nothing to render.

activities.title: Add an about page
activities.instruction: Create `app/about/page.js` exporting `AboutPage` that renders an `h1` with 'About us'.

teaching.text: Route segments are folders. The `page.js` file marks the segment as navigable; siblings without one are ignored by routing.
Name folders for URLs, not for the components inside. Renaming a folder changes a public URL.

lessons.task: Create app/about/page.js with an AboutPage component.
hints: The file lives at `app/about/page.js` and exports a component as default.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What URL does `app/shop/shoes/page.js` serve, and why?

lessons.title: 3. Layouts
lessons.summary: A layout wraps every page below it and keeps its state across navigation.

activities.title: The shell around the page
activities.instruction: The root layout must render `html` and `body`. It receives the current page as `children` and renders nav, fonts, and providers around it.

activities.title: Do layouts re-render?
activities.question: You navigate between two pages under the same layout. What happens to the layout?
choices: It stays mounted; only the page content swaps
activities.answer: It stays mounted; only the page content swaps
activities.explanation: That persistence is why layouts are the right place for navigation and providers — their state survives page changes.

activities.title: Root layout
activities.instruction: Write the root layout that renders `html` and `body` around `children`.

teaching.text: Layouts are shared UI. The root layout is required and must contain `html` and `body`; nested layouts wrap only their own segment.
Do not put `'use client'` on the root layout. It turns every page below it into a client boundary.

lessons.task: Write a root layout wrapping children in html and body.
hints: Destructure `children` from props and render it inside `<body>`.

<html lang="en">
  <body>{children}</body>
</html>
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is the root layout a bad place for a cart badge that should update on navigation?

lessons.title: 4. Navigating with Link
lessons.summary: Link navigates client-side without a full page reload.

activities.title: Client-side navigation
activities.instruction: `<Link href="...">` prefetches and swaps only the changed segment. A plain `<a>` makes the browser reload the whole app.

activities.title: Anchor vs Link
activities.question: What do you lose by using a plain `<a href="/about">` for internal navigation?
choices: Client-side navigation, prefetching, and preserved layout state
SEO, because crawlers cannot follow anchors
activities.answer: Client-side navigation, prefetching, and preserved layout state
activities.explanation: An anchor triggers a full document load. Next's Link keeps the React tree and prefetches the route in view.

activities.title: Link to about
activities.instruction: Import `Link` from `next/link` and render a nav with links to `/` and `/about`.

teaching.text: Link is the App Router's navigation primitive. It renders an anchor for accessibility and crawlers while intercepting the click for client-side routing.

import Link from 'next/link';

<Link href="/about">About</Link>
For programmatic navigation use `useRouter()` from `next/navigation`. The old `next/router` import fails in the App Router.

hints: Import the component first, then use it like an anchor with `href`.

import Link from 'next/link';

<Link href="/about">About</Link>
lessons.reflectionPrompt: When is a plain anchor still the correct choice inside a Next.js app?

tracks.name: Data & Loading States
tracks.description: Fetch on the server and give every slow or broken state a screen.

lessons.title: 5. Fetching in a server component
lessons.summary: Server components can await data directly, with no useEffect.

activities.title: Await in the component
activities.instruction: A server component may be `async`. Run the query with `await` before returning JSX; the HTML arrives already filled in.

activities.title: Why no useEffect
activities.question: Why is there no `useEffect` or loading flag in the example?
choices: The HTML is rendered on the server after the await resolves
activities.answer: The HTML is rendered on the server after the await resolves
activities.explanation: Server components render to HTML on the server, so the data is already there in the first response. A `loading.js` covers the wait.

activities.title: Server-side fetch
activities.instruction: Write an async default page component that fetches `https://api.example.com/products` and renders the product names in a list.

teaching.text: Server components run on the server and never ship to the browser. That makes them the default place for database and API access.
Next extends `fetch` with caching. Without `cache: 'no-store'` or `revalidate`, a fetch may be cached and serve stale data.

lessons.task: Fetch products in an async page component and render them.
hints: Mark the component `async` so you can `await` inside it.

const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/products');
const products = await res.json();
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What does the browser receive for this page, given the component never runs there?

lessons.title: 6. loading.js
lessons.summary: A sibling loading.js streams an instant placeholder while the page awaits data.

activities.title: A fallback per segment
activities.instruction: Drop `loading.js` next to a `page.js` and Next shows it while that segment renders. Returning skeleton markup instead of a spinner prevents layout shift.

activities.title: Where it applies
activities.question: What does `app/products/loading.js` cover?
choices: The /products segment, including its nested routes
activities.answer: The /products segment, including its nested routes
activities.explanation: A loading file wraps its segment and everything below it, unless a nested segment provides its own.

activities.title: Skeleton loader
activities.instruction: Create `app/products/loading.js` exporting `Loading` that renders a pulsing placeholder.

teaching.text: Streaming lets the server send the shell immediately and the data-filled page when it is ready. `loading.js` is the fallback in between.
Skeletons shaped like the real content read as fast. A centred spinner makes the page jump when content lands.

lessons.task: Add a loading component for the products segment.
hints: The file is a plain component with no data fetching.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does a skeleton usually feel faster than a spinner, even with identical timing?

lessons.title: 7. error.js
lessons.summary: An error boundary keeps a failed segment from taking down the page.

activities.title: Catch render errors
activities.instruction: `error.js` must be a client component. It receives `error` and a `reset` function that retries rendering the segment.

activities.title: Server or client
activities.question: Why must an error boundary be a client component?
choices: React catches render errors in the browser, which needs component state and effects
activities.answer: React catches render errors in the browser, which needs component state and effects
activities.explanation: The boundary subscribes to React's error lifecycle, which only exists in the client runtime.

activities.title: Retry screen
activities.instruction: Write `app/products/error.js` as a client component with an h2 and a button that calls `reset`.

teaching.text: Errors thrown while rendering a segment bubble to the nearest `error.js`. The rest of the layout stays alive.
Leaving `error.message` on screen leaks internals. Log the error, show a friendly line, and offer reset.

lessons.task: Add an error boundary for the products segment with a reset button.
hints: Start the file with `'use client'` and accept `{ error, reset }`.
<button onClick={() => reset()}>Try again</button>
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is showing the raw error message to users a security problem?

lessons.title: 8. Dynamic routes
lessons.summary: Brackets capture a URL segment, and params arrives as a promise in Next 15.

activities.title: Read the segment
activities.instruction: `[id]` captures that segment. In Next 15 the `params` prop is a promise, so `await` it before reading `id`.

activities.title: Async params
activities.question: In Next 15, what is `params` inside a page?
choices: A plain object with the route values
A promise that must be awaited
activities.answer: A promise that must be awaited
activities.explanation: Next 15 made `params` and `searchParams` async so the page can start streaming before they resolve. Reading `params.id` directly warns or fails.

activities.title: Product page
activities.instruction: Create `app/products/[id]/page.js` that awaits `params`, fetches that product, and renders its name in an `h1`.

teaching.text: Dynamic segments share one page file. The captured value tells the page which record to load.
A missing record should call `notFound()` from `next/navigation`, not render an empty page with a 200 status.

lessons.task: Build a dynamic product page that awaits params and fetches the product.
hints: Destructure `params` from props, then `const { id } = await params;`.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why should an unknown product id return notFound() instead of an empty page?

tracks.name: Mutations & Caching
tracks.description: Write endpoints, mutate from forms, and refresh cached data.

lessons.title: 9. GET route handlers
lessons.summary: A route.js file exports HTTP methods that back your API.

activities.title: Your own JSON endpoint
activities.instruction: `app/api/products/route.js` answers `/api/products`. Export a function per method and return a `Response` — `NextResponse.json()` is the convenience wrapper.

activities.title: Which export
activities.question: How does Next decide which HTTP methods `/api/products` supports?
choices: From the exported function names: GET, POST, DELETE
It accepts all methods by default
activities.answer: From the exported function names: GET, POST, DELETE
activities.explanation: Each exported method name becomes a handler. Methods you do not export answer 405.

activities.title: Products endpoint
activities.instruction: Create `app/api/products/route.js` exporting an async `GET` that returns a JSON array of products.

teaching.text: Route handlers are the App Router's server endpoints. They sit next to pages and use standard Request/Response objects.
Route handlers are not cached by default in Next 15. Say `export const dynamic = 'force-static'` if you really want static output.

lessons.task: Export a GET handler that returns JSON products.
hints: Import `NextResponse` from `next/server`.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: When would you fetch data directly in a server component instead of adding a route handler?

lessons.title: 10. POST route handlers
lessons.summary: Read the body from the Request and answer with an explicit status.

activities.title: Validate, store, answer 201
activities.instruction: The handler receives a standard `Request`. `await request.json()` parses the body; return `NextResponse.json(created, { status: 201 })`.

activities.title: Malformed JSON
activities.question: A client POSTs invalid JSON. What does `await request.json()` do?
choices: Throws, so the request fails with a 500 unless you catch it
activities.answer: Throws, so the request fails with a 500 unless you catch it
activities.explanation: Parsing can throw. Wrap it in try/catch and answer 400 — bad client input is not a server error.

activities.title: Create endpoint
activities.instruction: Export an async `POST` that reads `request.json()`, rejects a missing name with 400, and otherwise returns the product with status 201.

teaching.text: Route handlers use the web-standard Request and Response APIs. Picking the right status is part of the contract your client codes against.
Wrap `request.json()` in try/catch. Unhandled parse errors turn a client mistake into a 500 and a noisy log.

lessons.task: Export a POST handler that validates and returns 201.
hints: Take `request` as the argument and parse it with `await request.json()`.
return NextResponse.json(product, { status: 201 });
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is a JSON parse failure a 400 and not a 500?

lessons.title: 11. Server actions
lessons.summary: A server function called straight from a form, with no fetch in between.

activities.title: Mutate and revalidate
activities.instruction: A `'use server'` function runs on the server but can be passed to a form's `action`. After writing, call `revalidatePath` so the cached page shows the new data.

activities.title: Why revalidate
activities.question: The action writes to the database but does not revalidate. What does the user see next?
activities.explanation: The route's cached output is still valid, so Next serves it. Revalidation marks it stale so the next request re-renders.

activities.title: Create product action
activities.instruction: Write a server action `createProduct` that reads `name` from `formData`, writes it, and revalidates `/products`.

teaching.text: Server actions remove the hand-written fetch: the form posts to a function, the function runs on the server, and the UI refreshes.
A server action is a public endpoint. Validate the input and check the session, exactly as you would in an API route.

lessons.task: Write a server action that creates a product and revalidates the list.
hints: Start the file with `'use server'` and import `revalidatePath` from `next/cache`.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is a server action not automatically safe just because it is not imported by the client?

lessons.title: 12. Client components
lessons.summary: Interactivity needs a client boundary — the smallest one you can manage.

activities.title: Opt in to the browser
activities.instruction: Anything using state, effects, or event handlers needs `'use client'` at the top of its file. Keep the boundary around the form, not the whole page.

activities.title: Boundary cost
activities.question: What does putting `'use client'` at the top of the root layout do?
choices: Makes everything below it a client component, enlarging the JS bundle
activities.answer: Makes everything below it a client component, enlarging the JS bundle
activities.explanation: The directive marks the whole module graph below it. Server-only data access then disappears from those components.

activities.title: Search form
activities.instruction: Write a client `SearchBar` component with `useState`, an input bound to the value, and a form that prevents the default submit.

teaching.text: Server components cannot hold state or attach handlers. A client component is the seam where interactivity begins.
Push `'use client'` down the tree. A server page can render a client form without becoming one itself.

lessons.task: Write a client search bar with state and a submit handler.
hints: The directive must be the first line, before imports.

const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
<form onSubmit={(e) => { e.preventDefault(); onSearch(query); }}>
lessons.reflectionPrompt: How would you keep a page a server component while still giving the user an interactive search box?
